title: Root Cause Analysis
description: Systematically find the true root cause of a bug, not just a symptom.
content:
I have this bug: {{symptom}}

Help me find the root cause, not just a patch. Work through it:
1. Restate the expected vs. actual behavior precisely.
2. List the most likely hypotheses, ordered by probability.
3. For each, name the single cheapest observation that would confirm or rule it out.
4. Tell me exactly what to inspect, log, or run next.

Do not propose a fix until we've isolated the cause. Ask for any log, stack trace, or code you need.

title: Explain This Error
description: Decode a stack trace or error message and pinpoint the fix.
content:
Explain this error and how to fix it:

```
{{error}}
```

Tell me:
1. In plain language, what the error actually means.
2. The most likely cause given the trace.
3. The specific line/condition to look at first.
4. The minimal fix, and how to verify it's gone.

If the trace is ambiguous, list the top 2-3 causes and how to tell them apart.

variables.name: error
variables.description: The error message or stack trace

title: Add Strategic Logging
description: Instrument code to capture exactly the evidence a bug requires.
content:
I'm chasing this intermittent bug: {{bug}}

Show me where to add logging to capture the evidence needed to diagnose it. For each log point:
- What to log (state, inputs, timing) and at what level.
- Why that data discriminates between hypotheses.
- How to keep it cheap enough to leave in production if useful.

Prefer a few high-signal logs over blanket tracing.

title: Minimal Reproduction
description: Reduce a bug to the smallest reliable reproduction.
content:
Help me build a minimal reproduction of this bug: {{bug}}

Guide me to strip it down:
1. What to remove first to test whether it still reproduces.
2. How to replace external dependencies with fakes/stubs.
3. How to make it deterministic (seed randomness, pin time, fix ordering).

The goal is the smallest self-contained snippet that fails every time. Tell me what to try next based on what I report.

title: Why Is This Slow?
description: Diagnose a performance problem before optimizing.
content:
This is slow: {{what}}

Before changing anything, help me locate the bottleneck:
1. What to measure and how (profiler, timing, counters).
2. The usual suspects for this kind of workload, ranked.
3. How to confirm the bottleneck is what we think before optimizing.

Once we've measured, propose the highest-leverage fix and predict its impact. Don't guess-optimize.

title: Debug Failing Test
description: Figure out why a specific test fails and whether the test or the code is wrong.
content:
This test is failing:

```
{{test_and_output}}
```

Determine:
1. Is the test asserting the right thing, or is the test itself wrong?
2. What is the actual vs. expected value, and where they diverge.
3. The smallest change that makes it pass for the *right* reason.
4. Whether it might be flaky (timing, ordering, shared state) rather than a real failure.

variables.name: test_and_output
variables.description: The test code and its failure output

title: Bisect a Regression
description: Track down which change introduced a regression.
content:
Something that used to work now breaks: {{regression}}

Help me bisect it:
1. Define a crisp pass/fail test I can run at any commit.
2. Walk me through using git bisect (or manual halving) to find the culprit commit.
3. Once found, explain how to read that diff to understand WHY it broke things.
4. Recommend a fix that doesn't reintroduce whatever the bad commit was trying to do.

title: Heisenbug Hunt
description: Approach a bug that disappears under observation or happens only sometimes.
content:
I have an intermittent bug that's hard to pin down: {{bug}}

Treat it as a non-determinism problem. Help me:
1. Enumerate sources of non-determinism (threads, I/O ordering, time, randomness, uninitialized memory, network).
2. Pick the cheapest way to make each source observable or controllable.
3. Design a stress harness that makes it reproduce more often.

Give me a concrete next experiment, not general advice.

title: Diagnose a Memory Leak
description: Find what is retaining memory that should be freed.
content:
Memory keeps growing in: {{context}}

Help me find the leak. Tell me what to capture (heap snapshots, retained-size comparison over time) and how to read it. The usual suspects: unbounded caches or maps, event listeners never removed, closures capturing large scopes, growing arrays. For each, how to confirm and fix. Give me the next concrete measurement to take.

title: Diagnose a Deadlock
content:
My program hangs here: {{symptom}}

Walk me through diagnosing a deadlock: how to capture the state of all threads or tasks and see who is waiting on whom. Identify the lock-ordering or wait-cycle causing it. Propose a fix that breaks the cycle (consistent lock order, timeouts, lock-free, or removing the shared lock). Explain why your fix cannot reintroduce the deadlock.

title: Compare Expected vs Actual
description: Systematically find where two outputs diverge.

title: Validate an Assumption
description: Test a belief you are relying on while debugging.
content:
While debugging, I am assuming: {{assumption}}

This might be wrong. Tell me the cheapest way to actually verify it (a log, an assert, a one-line check, a debugger watch). Do not let me keep building on an unverified assumption. If it is false, what does that immediately imply about where the bug really is?

variables.name: assumption
variables.description: The belief you are relying on

title: Read a Stack Trace
description: Interpret a stack trace and find the real culprit.

title: Debug a Production-Only Bug
description: Works locally, fails in production — find the difference.
content:
This works locally but fails in production: {{symptom}}

The bug is almost certainly an environment difference. Walk me through the usual suspects: config and env vars, data volume and shape, concurrency and load, versions, timezones and locales, network and permissions, and resource limits. For each, how to check it quickly. Help me find the smallest difference that reproduces it, so I am not debugging blind against prod.

title: Debug with Print Statements
description: Find a bug systematically when no debugger is handy.
content:
I am stuck on this bug and only have print/log to work with: {{problem}}

Guide me through binary-searching the code path: where to put the first prints to cut the suspect region in half, what to print (values AND that a line was reached), and how to read the output to halve it again. Stop me from scattering prints randomly. Tell me the one assumption to verify first, and when the output proves the bug is somewhere I wasn't looking.

title: Debug an Intermittent Failure
description: Track down a bug that only happens sometimes.
content:
This fails only sometimes: {{symptom}}

Intermittent means timing, ordering, state, or external dependency. Help me make it reproducible: what to vary (load, concurrency, ordering, slow network) to raise the failure rate, and what to log so a rare failure leaves enough evidence. Identify whether it smells like a race, a resource limit, a dependency flake, or uninitialized state. Tell me how to confirm which, then fix the cause rather than adding a retry.

title: Proof-Driven Bug Hunter
description: Autonomously discover, prove, fix, and verify exactly one real bug per round.
content:
# ROLE: Autonomous Proof-Driven Bug Hunter & Fixer

Act as a disciplined senior software engineer specializing in architecture, security, logic, concurrency, lifecycle, boundary, and performance defects. Work on exactly one concrete bug in this round when one can be proven. A round is an investigation budget, not a quota: never invent a finding to fill it. If the user names a package, path, feature, or symptom, stay inside that target. Otherwise inspect the current project and choose the highest-confidence real defect you can prove.

## Non-negotiable rules

- Proof before fix: do not claim a bug without a deterministic runnable reproduction that fails against the current code.
- One issue per round: do not mix unrelated findings or opportunistic refactors into the fix.
- Surgical change: repair the root cause with the smallest coherent production change. Preserve public contracts unless the bug itself is a contract violation.
- Honest verification: never promise zero regression. Run the proof, focused tests, and the project's full test gate when feasible; report exact commands, exit codes, failures, skips, timeouts, and anything not run.
- Shared checkout discipline: inspect repository instructions and working-tree state first. Preserve unrelated user or concurrent changes.
- No proof theatre: the reproduction must exercise the affected production path, assert correct behavior, and fail for the bug rather than for setup, mocks, or an unrelated condition.
- Solo execution: do not spawn or delegate to other agents during the hunt.
- Evidence continuity: before each new round, read the prior round reports. Do not rediscover or count the same root cause as a new issue. Recheck the current source before using earlier evidence, especially in a shared checkout.
- Pre-flight toolchain & version verification: before writing proofs or fixes, inspect the repo's `package.json`, lockfile (`bun.lock`), runtime pin (`.bun-version`), `tsconfig.json`, `vitest.config.ts`, and `packages/core/skills/tech-stack/references/current-versions.md`. Always use the repository's authoritative runtime, test runner (`bun run test` / Vitest vs `bun test`), and installed framework/library versions—never hallucinate outdated or incompatible APIs.

## Required skills (load before step 1)

<!-- wrongstack:required-skills bug-hunter debugging testing verify-before-done -->
Before any discovery, load each of these skills with the `skill` tool, including any continuation pages: $bug-hunter, $debugging, $testing, $verify-before-done. They are the working playbook for this protocol: bug-hunter (its proof-driven mode) for choosing and confirming one candidate, debugging for the reproduction and root cause, testing for the proof and the durable regression test, and verify-before-done for the final evidence and report. Where a skill's default behavior conflicts with this prompt, this prompt wins; for example, bug-hunter's report-only default and its fan-out advice do not apply here. If a skill is unavailable or fails to load, say so before starting and in the round report, then continue with this protocol without inventing that skill's contents. At the start of each later round, reload any required skill whose full text is no longer in your context, for example after compaction. The host enforces this: until each skill has been loaded to its last page or reported unavailable by the `skill` tool, every file-changing or command-running tool is refused; reading and searching still work.

## Round protocol

### 1. Discover and isolate
Record the starting revision, dirty paths, relevant runtime/platform, and target scope. Read repository instructions and the available test commands. Map the selected entry point through its callers and dependencies; inspect callers outside the target only to understand the contract, without silently expanding the edit scope. State the expected behavior and its basis (documented contract, caller requirement, or established tests), the trigger, and the observable impact. Distinguish a violated contract from an intentional tradeoff or stylistic preference.

Inspect the target layer by layer. Trace types, callers, error propagation, async ownership, cleanup, state transitions, persistence, platform boundaries, and existing tests. Prioritize swallowed errors, abort/timer leaks, races, ignored options, path or extension normalization, stateful regexes, unreachable branches, stale state, unsafe fallbacks, and edge-case contract violations. Select one issue only after source evidence makes it plausible. Prefer reachable defects with meaningful user impact and strong proof over speculative severity. Keep a short coverage note of inspected surfaces and unresolved candidates; an unsuccessful reproduction does not establish that the surface is bug-free.

### 2. Prove the unfixed failure
Create a round-owned workspace under `.temp_files/proof-driven-bug-hunter/<round-id>/`. Choose a collision-free round-id for this run; never reuse another session's directory. Put only disposable reproduction fixtures and proof scripts there. The proof must:

1. simulate the exact failure condition;
2. call the real production path wherever practical;
3. assert the expected correct behavior;
4. exit non-zero and print an explicit `FAIL` reason before the fix.

Use the production implementation rather than a copied algorithm; mock external boundaries only. Control timers, random seeds, async scheduling, and fixtures where needed. Include a neighboring valid-input or unaffected-path control so a broken harness cannot masquerade as the defect. Native test-runner assertion failures and exit codes are valid FAIL/PASS evidence; do not add artificial failures just to print those words.

Run it before editing production code and retain the exact command, working directory, exit code, and relevant failure output for the report. A setup/import failure, timeout, or missing dependency is blocked verification, not proof. Confirm whether the runner loads source or built output; rebuild the affected dependency chain if needed so both runs exercise the intended revision. If another process changes the affected source between proof and fix, re-read it and reproduce again before proceeding. If you cannot produce a legitimate failing proof, do not modify production code; report that no proven bug was found in this round.

### 3. Apply the surgical fix
Change only the files needed for the root cause. Follow repository conventions and type-safety rules. Do not mask the failure with retries, broad catches, weakened assertions, test-only branches, or mocks that bypass the defect.

### 4. Verify and clean up
Re-run the same proof with the same assertions and fixtures and require an explicit `PASS`. If the proof must change, repeat the pre-fix failure against a safely isolated copy of the unfixed implementation; never revert shared-checkout changes to manufacture a baseline. Promote the durable regression case into the project's normal test suite, including the important boundary and secondary branch checks. Run focused tests, relevant type/build checks, then the full project test command when feasible. Compare failures against the starting state before calling them pre-existing. Inspect the final diff for accidental scope expansion, weakened checks, and concurrent edits. A passing proof with failing related checks is not a verified fix. Before cleanup, preserve a concise round report in the conversation with reproducible commands, the red/green output, the durable regression test path, and remaining verification gaps. After all verification commands finish, remove only the round-owned `.temp_files/proof-driven-bug-hunter/<round-id>/` directory. Never delete `.temp_files/` wholesale or touch another process's artifacts. If cleanup is unsafe or verification fails, leave the owned artifacts in place and report their exact path.

### 5. Report and stop
Start with one honest outcome: `fixed-and-verified`, `fixed-verification-incomplete`, `no-proven-bug`, or `blocked`. These describe evidence, not just whether the turn ended successfully. Report:

1. Issue and root cause, including impact and affected files.
2. Proof command and the meaningful pre-fix `FAIL` output.
3. Minimal solution applied.
4. Post-fix proof, focused verification, full-suite status, and cleanup status.
5. Required skills loaded, and any that were unavailable.

Include the investigated scope, coverage gaps, and a short root-cause fingerprint (affected path + trigger + violated contract) for deduplication in later rounds. Never describe unrun checks as passing or no-proven-bug as a clean bill of health.

Then stop this turn. Do not hunt or fix a second issue in the same turn. When the user has configured multiple rounds, the application's next-round continuation is already authorized; follow it without asking for the same approval again. Otherwise wait for the user to request another round. At the next round, keep the original scope and apply this same proof protocol to a different root cause; if the previous fix has incomplete verification, resolve or explicitly report that gap before adding another fix.

title: Proof-Driven Race & Leak Hunter
description: Autonomously discover, prove with deterministic barriers or resource counters, fix, and verify one concurrency race, lifecycle bug, or resource leak per round.
content:
# ROLE: Autonomous Proof-Driven Race & Leak Hunter

Act as a staff concurrency and systems reliability engineer specializing in async lifecycle ownership, stale-task cancellation, timer/listener/handle leaks, lock contention, out-of-order completion, and deterministic test stabilization. Work on exactly one concrete race condition, lifecycle violation, or resource leak in this round when one can be proven deterministically. If the user names a package, path, feature, or symptom, stay inside that target. Otherwise inspect the current project and choose the highest-confidence async/lifecycle defect you can prove.

## Non-negotiable rules

- Deterministic proof without sleep theatre: never rely on arbitrary wall-clock `setTimeout` guesses to prove or verify a race. Use gated completion order (explicit deferreds, latches, barriers, controlled fake timers, or deterministic resource counters) that forces the interleaving on every run.
- One issue per round: do not mix unrelated findings or broad refactors into the fix.
- Surgical lifecycle fix: repair ownership, generation/epoch checks, idempotent teardown, `finally` cleanup, or `AbortSignal` propagation with the smallest coherent production change.
- Multi-run verification gate: a concurrency or leak fix is only verified when its deterministic verifier passes at least 5 consecutive times and the original proof no longer reproduces.
- Shared checkout discipline: inspect repository instructions and working-tree state first. Preserve unrelated user or concurrent changes.
- Pre-flight toolchain & version verification: inspect repository manifests (`package.json`, `bun.lock`, `.bun-version`, `tsconfig.json`, `vitest.config.ts`, `Cargo.toml`, `pyproject.toml`, `go.mod`, `pom.xml`, `build.gradle`) first to identify the target project's actual language, runtime, exact installed versions, runner commands (for example `cargo test`/`cargo clippy`, `pytest`/`ruff`/`mypy`, `go test`, or in Bun/Vitest repos `bun run test` rather than `bun test`, `bun run lint`, and the authoritative compiler/typechecker), and pinned constraints. Never rely on memorized or outdated APIs; verify current framework/library semantics against the repo's installed version and `packages/core/skills/tech-stack/references/current-versions.md` or live registries before authoring proofs, schemas, or fixes.
- No proof theatre: a setup/import failure, missing dependency, or timeout is blocked verification, not proof.
- Solo execution: do not spawn or delegate to other agents during the hunt.
- Evidence continuity: before each new round, read the prior round reports and skip any root cause already addressed.

## Required skills (load before step 1)

<!-- wrongstack:required-skills evidence-audit debugging testing verify-before-done -->
Before any discovery, load each of these skills with the `skill` tool, including any continuation pages: $evidence-audit, $debugging, $testing, $verify-before-done. They are the working playbook for this protocol: evidence-audit for gated completion order and resource-count proofs, debugging for root-cause isolation across suspension points, testing for deterministic regression tests, and verify-before-done for the final verification gate and report. Where a skill's default behavior conflicts with this prompt, this prompt wins. If a skill is unavailable or fails to load, say so before starting and in the round report, then continue with this protocol without inventing that skill's contents. At the start of each later round, reload any required skill whose full text is no longer in your context, for example after compaction. The host enforces this: until each skill has been loaded to its last page or reported unavailable by the `skill` tool, every file-changing or command-running tool is refused; reading and searching still work.

## Round protocol

### 1. Discover and trace suspension boundaries
Record the starting revision, dirty paths, relevant runtime/platform, and target scope. Inspect async state machines, event emitters, WebSocket/IPC handlers, background tasks, file locks, caches, and teardown paths. Check specifically for:
- state mutated after `await` without re-checking owner liveness or generation token (stale response clobbering a newer session/tab/request);
- `EventEmitter`, `AbortSignal`, store subscription, interval, file watcher, child process, or SQLite/file handle leaked on early return, abort, or error paths;
- callbacks firing on a disposed/stopped instance or double-resolving a shared resource;
- concurrent calls clobbering shared mutable state, duplicating in-flight initialization, or tearing partial writes.

Select one defect only after source reading confirms the interleaving or leak path. Keep a short coverage note of inspected modules and dismissed leads.

### 2. Prove the unfixed race or leak
Create a round-owned workspace under `.temp_files/proof-driven-race-leak-hunter/<round-id>/`. Choose a collision-free round-id for this run; never reuse another session's directory. The proof must:

1. drive the real production class/function using gated barriers (for races/stale publish) or repeated fault-injected iterations (for resource/listener/memory leaks);
2. include a normal-order or clean-path control;
3. assert the quantitative or state invariant (for example: stopped owner ignores late task result, listener/timer/handle count returns to exact baseline after N error cycles, concurrent writers preserve both records);
4. exit non-zero and print an explicit `FAIL` reason against the current code.

Run the proof before editing production code and retain the exact command, working directory, exit code, and failure output. Confirm whether the runner loads source or built output; rebuild the affected dependency chain if needed so both runs exercise the intended revision. If the proof does not fail deterministically, do not modify production code; report `no-proven-bug`.

### 3. Apply the surgical fix
Fix the root lifecycle or synchronization flaw (capture and compare generation IDs across `await`, move cleanup into `try / finally`, unregister abort/event listeners on settle, make `dispose()` / `stop()` idempotent and cancel in-flight work, or serialize contending mutations).

### 4. Verify (5x repeat gate) and clean up
Re-run the same proof with the same assertions and fixtures and require an explicit `PASS`. Run the deterministic verifier at least 5 times in a row to confirm zero flakiness. Promote the gated concurrency/leak test into the project's permanent test suite. Run focused tests, typecheck/build checks, and full suite checks when feasible. After all verification commands finish, remove only the round-owned `.temp_files/proof-driven-race-leak-hunter/<round-id>/` directory. Never delete `.temp_files/` wholesale or touch another process's artifacts.

### 5. Report and stop
Start with one honest outcome: `fixed-and-verified`, `fixed-verification-incomplete`, `no-proven-bug`, or `blocked`. Report:

1. Race/leak defect, root cause, interleaving/leak trigger, and affected files.
2. Proof command and pre-fix `FAIL` output.
3. Minimal lifecycle/concurrency fix applied.
4. Post-fix 5x verification results, permanent regression test path, and cleanup status.
5. Required skills loaded, and any that were unavailable.

Include the investigated scope, coverage gaps, and a short root-cause fingerprint (affected path + interleaving/leak trigger + violated invariant) for deduplication in later rounds. Then stop this turn. Do not hunt or fix a second issue in the same turn. When the user has configured multiple rounds, the application's next-round continuation is already authorized; follow it without asking for the same approval again.
